metadata.name: dynamodb
metadata.overview:
Amazon DynamoDB is a serverless, fully managed NoSQL database service. It supports both key-value and document data models and delivers consistent single-digit millisecond response times. Storage and throughput scale automatically with demand, with no servers to provision, patch, or maintain, and no maintenance windows or version upgrades.

Applications store schemaless records addressed by a primary key, so the data model can evolve without redefining a rigid schema. Alternate keys let applications query the same data along additional access patterns, and vector indexes support similarity search over embeddings. Transactions apply coordinated, all-or-nothing changes across multiple records. Change data capture emits a near-real-time, time-ordered feed of record-level modifications for event-driven processing, and per-record expiration timestamps remove stale data automatically.

DynamoDB replicates data across multiple Availability Zones for durability and availability, and can maintain multi-active replicas across AWS Regions so globally distributed applications read and write locally. Continuous and on-demand backups support recovery from unintended changes and long-term retention. Data is encrypted at rest and in transit, access is governed through AWS identity and resource policies with item- and attribute-level conditions, and traffic can be confined to private network paths.
useCases: Financial services platforms running transaction ledgers, payments, loan management, token generation and fraud detection, where all-or-nothing multi-item transactions, strong read consistency and multi-Region resilience are required to keep the system correct and available during regional impairment.

entities.name: Backup
entities.overview:
An Amazon DynamoDB backup is a full, self-contained snapshot of one table's data at a point in time. It captures every item together with the table's secondary indexes, stream settings, and throughput configuration. Creating a backup does not interrupt the table and does not draw on its read or write capacity.

Backups address long-term retention, archival, and regulatory record-keeping needs that a rolling recovery window cannot cover. A backup persists until it is explicitly deleted, so retention is entirely under your control. DynamoDB also creates a snapshot automatically when a table with point-in-time recovery enabled is deleted, preserving a recovery path for that table. Backup data is always encrypted, using the encryption key that protected the source table when the snapshot was taken.

Recovering from a backup always produces a new table instead of overwriting an existing one. The restore can target the original Region or a different one, and can adjust secondary indexes, capacity mode, and encryption settings. Operational and security settings such as access policies, tags, expiry rules, and recovery settings are not carried across and must be reapplied on the restored table.

entities.name: GlobalTable
entities.overview:
A DynamoDB global table joins DynamoDB tables in different AWS Regions into one replication group. Each member table, called a replica, stores the same complete set of items. An application can read from and write to any replica, and DynamoDB propagates each write to the replicas in the other Regions.

Global tables help applications serve users from a nearby Region with local read and write latency. They also place a full copy of the workload's data in each participating Region, so traffic can be redirected when one Region becomes degraded. Writes made while a Region is unreachable are tracked and propagated once it returns. Concurrent updates to the same item in different Regions are reconciled on a last-writer-wins basis, so replicas converge on identical data.

This is the earlier global tables design. Empty replica tables are created in each Region first, then joined into a named replication group. Every participating table must share the same name and primary key, and must emit a change stream carrying both old and new item images. The later design, which manages replicas directly through the table, is recommended instead. It synchronizes settings such as encryption, time to live, capacity, and secondary indexes across replicas, supports adding replicas to tables that already hold data, and is available in more Regions.

entities.name: Stream
entities.overview:
An Amazon DynamoDB stream captures item-level changes to a table as an ordered log of change records. Every write, update, and delete on the table appears in the stream in near-real time. Applications read these records to drive event-driven processing, cross-Region replication, archiving, and near-real-time analytics.

A stream belongs to one table and is turned on through that table's configuration. You choose how much of each changed item a record carries: keys only, the prior image, the new image, or both. Records are grouped into shards that DynamoDB creates and splits automatically as table throughput grows. Records are retained for a fixed window and then trimmed, so consumers must keep pace with the stream.

Because records can carry complete item images, a stream is a separate data path that warrants its own access controls. It has its own resource identifier and accepts a resource-based policy and tags independently of the parent table. This lets you grant change-data consumers read access to the stream without granting access to the table itself.

entities.name: Table
entities.overview:
An Amazon DynamoDB table is the primary container for data in DynamoDB. It stores a collection of items, and each item is a set of attributes. Every item is addressed by a primary key, either a partition key alone or a partition key combined with a sort key. Apart from the key, tables are schemaless, so each item can carry its own attributes.

Tables support key-value and document access patterns with consistent low-latency reads and writes. Secondary indexes let applications query the same data using alternate keys. Capacity scales automatically or can be provisioned, and no servers or software need managing. Tables suit applications that need predictable performance as data volume and request rates grow.

A table is the unit at which DynamoDB applies data protection and access control. Encryption at rest always applies to table data, and the encryption key can be an AWS owned, AWS managed, or customer managed key. Access is governed entirely through IAM, including item-level and attribute-level conditions and resource-based policies. Tables also anchor continuous and on-demand backups, time-to-live expiry, change data capture, cross-Region replication, and import and export to object storage.

mitigations.statement: Amazon DynamoDB service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made against trusted resources or AWS service-owned resources

mitigationContext.context: You can call the Amazon DynamoDB API from your VPC through a gateway VPC endpoint or an interface VPC endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink. Restricting those calls to resources in your organization enforces the resource perimeter on your network.

mitigations.statement: Amazon DynamoDB service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made by trusted identities or AWS services

mitigationContext.context: You can call the Amazon DynamoDB API from your VPC through a gateway VPC endpoint or an interface VPC endpoint powered by AWS PrivateLink. Restricting those calls to principals in your organization enforces the identity perimeter on your network.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB global table should be replicated to at least one other AWS Region

mitigationContext.context: A global table in Amazon DynamoDB is a set of replica tables in different AWS Regions that each hold the same data items. Writes to one replica are propagated automatically to the other replicas.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB stream should be accessed only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: Requests to your Amazon DynamoDB stream can originate from any network, including unexpected networks, and are authorized separately from requests to its parent table. A network perimeter helps you confirm that your stream can be accessed only from expected networks.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon DynamoDB stream resources

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on an Amazon DynamoDB stream in another account can grant your identities read access to its change-data-capture records. A resource perimeter helps confirm that your identities read those records only from streams your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB stream's resource-based policy should limit permissions to a subset of IAM principals, rather than granting access to all IAM principals

mitigationContext.context: You can attach a resource-based policy to your stream, and its `$.Policy` document names the IAM principals allowed to read stream records. A wildcard principal in that document can extend that access to every IAM principal in an account or organization.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB stream should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: A DynamoDB stream supports its own resource-based policy, attached directly to the stream. The policy can extend access to accounts outside your organization.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB stream should be governed by a policy that requires all connections to be encrypted in transit

mitigationContext.context: The DynamoDB Streams endpoint accepts both HTTP and HTTPS requests, so requests for your stream records can arrive unencrypted. DynamoDB supports resource-based policies on streams.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB stream should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: A DynamoDB stream is independently taggable through its own stream ARN, so you can record owner and purpose directly on the stream. Stream tags are not inherited from the parent table.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB stream should be configured to disallow resource-based policy modifications that would remove all policy-management access for the stream

mitigationContext.context: A DynamoDB stream carries its own resource-based policy that can govern the `dynamodb:PutResourcePolicy` action needed to amend that policy. DynamoDB rejects a policy that removes your own policy-management access, unless the request explicitly confirms that removal.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should be accessed only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: Requests to your Amazon DynamoDB table can originate from any network, including unexpected networks. A network perimeter helps you confirm that your table can be accessed only from expected networks.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should have point-in-time recovery enabled

mitigationContext.context: DynamoDB provides point-in-time recovery for the items a table persists, through a native backup capability on the table's own API. The recovery window is configurable from 1 to 35 days, with per-second restore granularity.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon DynamoDB table resources

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on an Amazon DynamoDB table in another account can grant your identities access to the table and its items. A resource perimeter helps confirm that your identities read and write items only in tables your organization owns.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should be protected by an AWS Backup backup plan

mitigationContext.context: Amazon DynamoDB is natively integrated with AWS Backup, which supports a table as an independently protectable resource type. A table is the primary store for your persisted data, and AWS Backup captures its contents in recovery points that you can restore to a new table.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon DynamoDB table lets you select a customer managed key for its server-side encryption at rest through `$.SSESpecification.KMSMasterKeyId`. Owning the key gives you control over its policy and lifecycle, audit of its use, and the ability to make table data unavailable.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table's resource policy should limit permissions to a subset of IAM principals, rather than granting access to all IAM principals

mitigationContext.context: Your DynamoDB table supports a resource-based policy that must specify a principal. A wildcard principal in that policy extends its DynamoDB permissions to every IAM principal.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should be replicated to at least one other AWS Region

mitigationContext.context: A DynamoDB table is a Regional resource that persists your items and attributes. Global tables provide AWS-managed replication of that table data to replicas in other AWS Regions.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: A DynamoDB table supports a resource-based policy that grants permissions to perform actions on the table. That policy can grant those permissions to principals outside your organization, making the identity perimeter applicable to this table.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should be accessed by an AWS service principal, such as the Amazon Redshift service principal, only when the service principal is acting on behalf of a trusted resource, AWS account, or organization

mitigationContext.context: A resource-based policy on your DynamoDB table can grant an AWS service principal, such as `redshift.amazonaws.com`, access to the table. Such a grant may raise the cross-service confused deputy problem, where that principal may be able to act on behalf of resources outside your organization.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should be governed by a policy that requires all connections to be encrypted in transit

mitigationContext.context: Amazon DynamoDB supports resource-based policies on tables. Encrypted connections are a client-side default rather than a table-side requirement, so a policy can require encryption in transit.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: Your Amazon DynamoDB table accepts tags at creation through the tag key and value parameters `$.Tags[*].Key` and `$.Tags[*].Value`. You can also tag the table after creation by calling `TagResource` against its own ARN.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should be configured to disallow table policy modifications that would remove all policy-management access for the table

mitigationContext.context: Your DynamoDB table supports a resource-based policy, known as a table policy, that governs the `dynamodb:PutResourcePolicy` and `dynamodb:DeleteResourcePolicy` actions on the table itself. A policy write can therefore leave no principal able to change the table policy, and `PutResourcePolicy` accepts `$.x-amz-confirm-remove-self-resource-access` to waive that self-access-removal guard.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should have CloudWatch Contributor Insights enabled to collect detailed CloudWatch metrics

mitigationContext.context: Your DynamoDB table supports CloudWatch Contributor Insights, an optional monitoring feature that publishes detailed metrics to CloudWatch. You can configure the feature for each table you manage.

If another monitoring platform already collects equivalent detailed metrics for this resource, that platform can provide the same visibility for anomaly detection and incident response. Enable this feature when no equivalent collection is in place.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon DynamoDB table should have deletion protection enabled

mitigationContext.context: Deleting an Amazon DynamoDB table cannot be undone, and data is recoverable only where backups or point-in-time recovery exist. The table supports a built-in deletion protection capability that helps protect it from unintended deletion.

threats.prerequisites: operating from a governed VPC network
threats.threatAction: can use the governed VPC network to make Amazon DynamoDB service API calls

threatContext.context: An IAM principal from outside your organization can reach the Amazon DynamoDB API from your VPC. That access enables transfer of data from your VPC to DynamoDB tables in an AWS account outside your organization.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on untrusted Amazon DynamoDB resources
threats.threatAction: can interact with those untrusted resources from a governed VPC network

threatContext.context: An IAM principal in your VPC can access an Amazon DynamoDB table in an account outside your organization. That access enables reading data from that table or transferring data from your VPC into it.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify or delete an Amazon DynamoDB global table
threats.threatAction: can delete the global table by removing all of its replicas, stopping cross-Region replication and removing multi-Region read and write availability

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to modify or delete an Amazon DynamoDB global table can remove all of its replica Regions. Removing every replica deletes the global table and stops cross-Region replication and multi-Region read and write availability.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify a resource-based policy governing an Amazon DynamoDB stream
threats.threatAction: can make the stream inaccessible by modifying the stream resource-based policy

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to modify the stream resource-based policy can call `PutResourcePolicy` with a policy that blocks stream reads. That policy can also block later changes to itself, leaving the stored change log unreachable.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon DynamoDB stream
threats.threatAction: can configure the stream without required tagging information

threatContext.context: A principal that manages a DynamoDB stream can do so without applying the tags your organization requires for that stream. The stream may then fall outside your tag-based cost allocation and ownership tracking.

threats.prerequisites: with a method for enumerating public Amazon DynamoDB streams, or prior knowledge of an existing public stream
threats.threatAction: can access a stream that has been configured to allow public access and read the item-level change records it retains for the parent table

threatContext.context: The resource-based policy on your stream can grant its read actions, such as `dynamodb:GetRecords`, to principals outside your organization. Those principals can then read the item-level change records the stream retains, without holding any permission on the parent table.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on an untrusted Amazon DynamoDB stream
threats.threatAction: can interact with the untrusted stream, including sending data to it or receiving data from it

threatContext.context: Amazon DynamoDB streams support cross-account access granted through their resource-based policies. An IAM principal in your organization can therefore read item-level change records from a stream owned by an account outside your organization.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to read or modify my Amazon DynamoDB stream and access to an unexpected network
threats.threatAction: can interact with my stream from an unexpected network

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with valid credentials can initiate requests against your Amazon DynamoDB stream from an unexpected network. From that network, a principal with permissions on the stream can read item-level change records, or rewrite or remove its resource-based policy.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon DynamoDB stream through its resource-based policy
threats.threatAction: can use my stream

threatContext.context: A resource-based policy on your stream can grant read access to identities outside your organization. Those identities can then call `GetShardIterator` and `GetRecords` to read the item-level change records the stream retains for 24 hours.

threats.prerequisites: with network adjacency to the connection path between clients and an Amazon DynamoDB stream that has not been configured to encrypt data in transit
threats.threatAction: can capture stream network traffic and read data in transit that has not been encrypted

threatContext.context: Clients consume your stream by calling `DescribeStream`, `GetShardIterator` and `GetRecords` across a network path. When a connection is not encrypted, a threat actor adjacent to that path can read those exchanges and the stream records they return.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to delete an Amazon DynamoDB table
threats.threatAction: can delete the table and the items that the table contains

threatContext.context: A single `DeleteTable` call removes the table and all of the items it holds. The caller needs only the table name in `$.TableName`, not an item-level permission such as `dynamodb:DeleteItem`.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify a resource-based policy governing an Amazon DynamoDB table
threats.threatAction: can make the table inaccessible by modifying the table resource-based policy

threatContext.context: A principal with permission to call `PutResourcePolicy` can replace the resource-based policy on your table with one that blocks access for all principals. The table and its stored items remain in place, but legitimate principals can no longer reach them.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to delete the AWS KMS customer managed key used by an Amazon DynamoDB table
threats.threatAction: can delete the AWS KMS customer managed key used by the table, which drives the table to `INACCESSIBLE_ENCRYPTION_CREDENTIALS`, blocks all reads and writes, and archives the table so that its items, secondary indexes, stream and backups can no longer be accessed

threatContext.context: When your DynamoDB table uses a customer managed key, its items, secondary indexes, stream and backups all depend on that one key. An IAM principal with permissions to delete that key can render the table and its backups inaccessible.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an Amazon DynamoDB table's CloudWatch Contributor Insights
threats.threatAction: can disable CloudWatch Contributor Insights for the table, deleting the per-key insight rules and stopping publication of the `ConsumedThroughputUnits` and `ThrottleCount` metrics

threatContext.context: CloudWatch Contributor Insights adds per-key metrics for your DynamoDB table beyond the default table-level metrics. A principal with permission to call `UpdateContributorInsights` can disable it, deleting the insight rules and stopping publication of those metrics.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify data in an Amazon DynamoDB table
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the items and attributes stored in the table with key material outside the AWS account owner's control

threatContext.context: An IAM principal calling `CreateTable` or `UpdateTable` can set `$.SSESpecification.KMSMasterKeyId` to a key with imported key material or an external key store. The holder of that key material can delete it or disconnect the external key store, leaving your table archived and unreadable.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon DynamoDB table
threats.threatAction: can configure the table without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal can create a table without the required tags, or remove those tags later by calling `UntagResource`. A table left without those tags may fall outside the ownership attribution processes that key on tags.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon DynamoDB table
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the table with an AWS owned or AWS managed KMS key, limiting your ability to govern the key's policy and lifecycle

threatContext.context: An IAM principal who can create or modify your table also selects the AWS KMS key type that protects it at rest. Both the default AWS owned key and the AWS managed key limit your governance of the key's policy and lifecycle.

threats.prerequisites: with a method for enumerating public Amazon DynamoDB tables, or prior knowledge of an existing public table
threats.threatAction: can access a table that has been configured to allow public access

threatContext.context: A DynamoDB table can be configured to allow access from any AWS account rather than a defined set of identities. A threat actor with knowledge of such a table can read your items with `dynamodb:Scan` or export them with `dynamodb:ExportTableToPointInTime`.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon DynamoDB table that supports CloudWatch Contributor Insights
threats.threatAction: can create or configure the table without CloudWatch Contributor Insights enabled

threatContext.context: `CreateTable` exposes no Contributor Insights parameter, so a new DynamoDB table starts without per-partition-key `ConsumedThroughputUnits` and `ThrottleCount` metric series. Without that per-key detail, concentrated key access or whole-table enumeration through `Scan` blends into table-level aggregates.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on an untrusted Amazon DynamoDB table
threats.threatAction: can interact with the untrusted table, including sending data to it or receiving data from it

threatContext.context: Amazon DynamoDB tables support cross-account access granted through their resource-based policies. An IAM principal in your organization can therefore read items from, or write items to, a table owned by an account outside your organization.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on my Amazon DynamoDB table and access to an unexpected network
threats.threatAction: can interact with my table from an unexpected network

threatContext.context: Amazon DynamoDB authorizes requests to your table on the signed IAM credential, not on the network a request comes from. An IAM principal with permissions on the table can read, modify, and export items from an unexpected network, or reconfigure and delete the table.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read items from an Amazon DynamoDB table that has not been encrypted at rest with a KMS customer managed key
threats.threatAction: can read plaintext items in the table, including harvesting every attribute of every item through `Scan` or a PartiQL statement

threatContext.context: Without a customer managed key, your table's items are encrypted under an AWS owned key you cannot audit or disable. A principal with data-plane read permissions can call `Scan` or `ExecuteStatement` and read plaintext items.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon DynamoDB table through its resource-based policy
threats.threatAction: can use my table

threatContext.context: A resource-based policy on your Amazon DynamoDB table can grant DynamoDB actions on the table and its items to identities outside your organization. DynamoDB enforces such cross-account grants, allowing those identities to read, change, or delete your table data.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to delete items from an Amazon DynamoDB table
threats.threatAction: can delete items from the table while the table itself remains intact and continues serving requests

threatContext.context: Amazon DynamoDB exposes item-level delete operations on your table, including `DeleteItem`, `BatchWriteItem` and PartiQL `DELETE` statements. An IAM principal granted actions such as `dynamodb:DeleteItem` can delete items while the table remains intact and continues serving requests.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read items from an Amazon DynamoDB table that is encrypted with an AWS managed KMS key in the same account as the principal
threats.threatAction: can read the items in the table

threatContext.context: Your table can be encrypted with the AWS managed key `aws/dynamodb`, whose key policy AWS establishes and you do not manage. IAM permissions for read actions such as `dynamodb:GetItem`, `dynamodb:Query`, and `dynamodb:Scan` then govern which principals in your account retrieve plaintext items.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read items from an Amazon DynamoDB table that has been encrypted with an AWS owned KMS key
threats.threatAction: can read items in the table in plaintext, because decryption is transparent to the caller and the AWS owned KMS key provides no additional authorization barrier

threatContext.context: Your table stores items encrypted at rest with an AWS owned KMS key whenever no encryption type is specified. That key type gives you no key policy to govern, no audit record of key use, and no control over the key lifecycle.
